title: Chris Hemsworth Can Lift More Weight than Me
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Using a tongue-in-cheek comparison of himself to Chris Hemsworth, Stuart makes a serious point about the wide range of preparedness teachers encounter in any classroom, and how two ideas from learning science help him respond to it: students grow through the exertion of good effort on well-chosen exercises, and mental and physical effort is a finite resource. He argues these two principles apply regardless of where a student starts; every student can improve through good effort applied to the right work, but no student can exert unlimited effort in a single day. This finitude is, for Stuart, motivating rather than discouraging: because effort is limited, each day and each lesson represents a real, non-recoverable opportunity, similar to a missed gym session that can't simply be made up by doubling up tomorrow. He closes with three practical takeaways centered on providing the right work, stewarding students' finite effort well, and treating each lesson as consequential.
points: Two learning-science principles anchor the piece: effort is productive, students of any starting point can improve through good effort on good exercises, and effort is finite, no student can exert unlimited mental or physical effort in a day.

Stuart uses the effort-is-finite principle to argue that lost instructional days can't simply be made up later, much like a missed gym session can't be recovered by lifting weights nonstop the next week.

The piece frames wide-ranging classroom preparedness, urban or rural, remedial or gifted, as less relevant than these two shared cognitive constraints, which apply to every student regardless of starting point.

Practical takeaway: because each day matters and effort must be stewarded well, the quality of the right work assigned on any given day directly determines how much of a student's limited effort translates into real growth.
quotes: In every single school I've visited, I've yet to find a teacher who doesn't struggle with the RANGE of students we teach. Urban or rural, affluent or free/reduced lunch, remedial or gifted — no matter the label, we've got learners coming to us with different degrees of preparedness, ability, willingness, and so on.
Thankfully, there are two ideas from the science of learning that really help: First, learners grow through the exertion of good effort on good exercises. Second, mental effort is a limited resource.
Neither of us is capable of infinite effort in a gym session. In other words, physical effort is a limited resource — even if you're Chris Hemsworth with biceps as big as DSJ.
This is hugely motivating to me. It means that each day matters greatly. To blow a lesson off is to blow off a precious opportunity to learn. It's to skip a trip to the gym.
I CAN'T do that because my effort is finite. Today, I'm capable of only so much of it. I've got to invest that well, and then come back tomorrow and do the same, and so on.
